## Week 2 {.center}

### Six questions for reading a Methods section

**Know what you are trying to rebuild, before you try to rebuild it.**

- The six questions are the **spine**; the NHANES anatomy is what the answers are
  **made of**
- Everything named today — component files, variable names, the join key — you use on
  **Thursday** in L1, and again for **M0** (due Wk3)

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Timing: per-slide markers in these notes sum to 144 min including the break,
against a 150-minute cap. Unlike the previous version of this deck, the markers now
include the interactive moments — the two vote-and-argue slides and the lab preview —
so the total is what actually happens in the room rather than content plus unbudgeted
discussion. Roughly 6 minutes of slack. The lecture plan carries the identical split;
if you retime a slide, retime it in both files. The plan also lists which slides to
drop first if you are running behind.
:::

## Why the question comes before the data

- The instinct is "what did they run?" — a model family answers nothing on its own
- A **Cox model appears under several different research goals**
- Reading a Methods section *is* the first act of reproduction

*By the end of today: this paper answers four of six questions clearly, one partially, and
one not at all.*

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Set the frame. Resist the urge to jump to the model. Tell them the scoreboard up
front — four clear, one partial, one unanswered — so they are listening for which is which.
:::

## The six questions {.center}

1. What is the **research goal**?
2. Who is the **population**, and how is eligibility operationalised?
3. What is the **exposure / index factor**, and the comparison?
4. What is the **outcome**, time zero, and follow-up?
5. What **other variables** enter, and what role are they supposed to play?
6. What **design and analysis features** must be respected?

> **If any one is under-specified, the study is not reconstructable — no matter how clean
> the results look.**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Keep this slide reachable all session; every section fills one row. Stress that these
are not this paper's questions — they are the template students take to their own M0
candidates. This replaces the old "four primitives", which asked what variables exist but
never what question they were meant to answer.
:::

# Q1 — What is the research goal?

## The paper states two aims, not one

- **Aim 1** — the *clinical correlates* of four groups defined by BMI and waist-to-height ratio
- **Aim 2** — the *prognostic value* of that classification for mortality

|  | Clinical correlates | Mortality prognosis |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | How do the four groups differ in health characteristics? | Do the four groups have different subsequent mortality? |
| **Time structure** | Cross-sectional at baseline | Longitudinal follow-up |

A single paper can carry more than one research question, and they have different clocks.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Read both aims off the abstract. The point is textual, not critical. The two rows
have different time structures, which is why one of them needs the linked mortality file
and the other does not.
:::

## Five goals the same variables can serve

| Research goal | Scientific target in this example |
|---|---|
| **Description** | What are the characteristics and mortality experience of each phenotype group? |
| **Association** | Is phenotype statistically associated with subsequent mortality? |
| **Prognostic factor** | Does phenotype carry information **over and above** other known prognostic factors? |
| **Prediction** | How accurately can we predict an individual's risk, and does adding WHtR improve it? |
| **Causal** | What would mortality have been under a specified contrast that changed central adiposity? |

> The variables can be identical. **The target quantity is not.**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Walk the ladder. Same exposure, same outcome, same covariates — five different
target quantities. Ask which row a "multivariable Cox model" sits on: it sits on several.
:::

## Same variables, different analyses

| Goal | Typical analysis | How are other variables handled? |
|---|---|---|
| **Description** | Weighted means, proportions; Kaplan–Meier or standardised survival | Stratification / standardisation where useful |
| **Association** | Cox regression, splines, group comparisons | Define a **conditional association**; no automatic causal reading |
| **Prognostic factor** | Cox model holding established prognostic factors + the index factor | Adjust for **other prognostic factors** |
| **Prediction** | Develop/validate a survival model; base vs base + WHtR | Chosen for predictive value; shrinkage and validation |
| **Causal** | Target trial; standardisation, g-formula, IPW | Select **confounders** by causal knowledge; avoid mediators/colliders |

> A Cox model appears in several rows. **The model family does not determine the goal.**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) This is the slide that kills "they ran a Cox model, so it is an association study".
Point out that the third and fifth rows can produce the identical R call and mean entirely
different things.
:::

## Same variables, different evidence of success

| Goal | What would count as evidence |
|---|---|
| **Description** | Absolute summaries with uncertainty: means, prevalences, survival at meaningful times |
| **Association** | An association measure such as HR + 95% CI; assumptions and functional form |
| **Prognostic factor** | Adjusted effect; for *incremental* value, a model with vs without the factor |
| **Prediction** | **Calibration**, **discrimination** (C-index / time-dependent AUC), **Brier score**, validation |
| **Causal** | A prespecified contrast, positivity/balance diagnostics, sensitivity to unmeasured confounding |

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The heart of Q1. The gap between a stated goal and the supplied evidence is
invisible unless you ask what evidence each goal would require. Do not rush this table —
students will reuse it at M0 and M1.
:::

## HR + CI: what it is, and is not, evidence for

**HR + CI** is enough to report an adjusted association, or a prognostic-factor effect.

It is **not** evidence that a prediction model is good, and **not** by itself evidence
that a causal effect has been identified.

*The paper names "prognostic value" and supplies adjusted association.*

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Keep this short and blunt. It is the one-line version of the previous table.
:::

## What does this paper most directly support?

**It directly supports:** description of how the groups differ; association between
phenotype and subsequent mortality; an adjusted prognostic association.

**It does not, by itself, establish:** that central adiposity *causes* the difference;
that reducing WHtR would reduce mortality; that adding WHtR improves individual prediction.

::: {.notes}
(2 min) **Vote and argue.** Which row of the ladder is this paper actually on? Take a show
of hands before revealing the second half. Do not resolve it for them too quickly — the
disagreement is the point, and it comes back at M1.
:::

# Q2 — Who is the population?

## First: how NHANES is organised

- **Six two-year cycles**, 2007–2018, each with its own file suffix: `E F G H I J`
- Files are **`.XPT`** (SAS transport) — `haven::read_xpt()`, or `nhanesA::nhanes()`
- Each file is **one row per participant, for one topic** — not one big table
- Three collection settings: **Interview** (home) · **MEC exam** (measured body size, BP) ·
  **Laboratory** (triglycerides, GGT, glucose)

| Family | Examples | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| Demographics | `DEMO` | age, sex, race, survey design, weights |
| Examination | `BMX`, `BPX` | measured body size, blood pressure |
| Laboratory | `TRIGLY`, `BIOPRO`, `GLU`, `GHB`, `HDL` | blood results |
| Questionnaire | `ALQ`, `BPQ`, `DIQ`, `SMQ` | self-reported history and medication |

> Mortality is **not** an NHANES file. It is a separate linked, fixed-width file from NCHS.

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Spend real time here. Everything in the rest of the lecture is a row in one of
these families, and on Thursday they type these names. The suffix letters are the single
most useful thing on the slide: H = 2013–2014, I = 2015–2016, J = 2017–2018.
:::

## Where the measurements and labs come from

| Concept | NHANES variable | Component |
|---|---|---|
| Participant ID | `SEQN` | *every file — the merge key* |
| Age, sex, race | `RIDAGEYR`, `RIAGENDR`, `RIDRETH3` | `DEMO` |
| BMI, waist, height | `BMXBMI`, `BMXWAIST`, `BMXHT` | `BMX` |
| Triglycerides | `LBXTR` | `TRIGLY` |
| GGT | `LBXSGTSI` | `BIOPRO` |
| Glucose, HbA1c | `LBXGLU`, `LBXGH` | `GLU`, `GHB` |
| HDL cholesterol | `LBDHDD` | `HDL` |
| Blood pressure | `BPXSY1–4`, `BPXDI1–4` | `BPX` |

Anthropometry, blood pressure and laboratory values are **measured or assayed**. Age, sex
and race/ethnicity come from the demographic file.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Do not read the table aloud. Ask instead: which of these is the exposure built
from, and which is eligibility built from? They will need both answers in Q3, and the fact
that the two lists overlap is the whole of slide "Eligibility and exposure share their
inputs".
:::

## Where the questionnaire, design and outcome come from

| Concept | NHANES variable | Component |
|---|---|---|
| BP / lipid medication | `BPQ050A`, `BPQ100D` | `BPQ` |
| Diabetes | `DIQ010`, `DIQ050`, `DIQ070` | `DIQ` |
| Alcohol | `ALQ130`, `ALQ120Q`, `ALQ120U`, `ALQ121` | `ALQ` |
| Survey design | `WTMEC2YR`, `WTSAF2YR`, `SDMVSTRA`, `SDMVPSU` | `DEMO`, `TRIGLY` |
| Mortality | `MORTSTAT`, `PERMTH_EXM`, `ELIGSTAT` | linked mortality file |

> These variables alone reach across **seven examination and laboratory components**, plus
> demographics, plus questionnaire components, plus a separate linked mortality file.
> **That is what L1 assembles.**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The last row is the one to dwell on: the outcome does not live in NHANES at all.
Students who assume one download gives them a study will lose a day to this. Note also
that the fasting weight `WTSAF2YR` ships on `TRIGLY`, not on `DEMO` — a design variable
living in a laboratory file.
:::

## SEQN is the join key

- Every respondent has one **`SEQN`** — the identifier CDC uses to sort and merge files
- Analysis = pick the topic files you need, **merge on `SEQN`**, one row per person
- SEQN does **not** repeat across the continuous cycles: all **59,842** values across
  2007–2018 are distinct, and the per-cycle ranges do not overlap
  — *Analysis set: all NHANES 2007–2018 records, N = 59,842*
- The ranges are **not contiguous**, though — a gap of 1,640 sits between 2011–2012 and
  2013–2014, so do not infer a cycle from an ID
- Keep a **cycle variable** anyway: provenance, definitions that change between cycles,
  and weights built per cycle. Not to disambiguate SEQN

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Correct a common belief here: students are often told to build a composite key
because SEQN "repeats". It does not. Checked against the raw DEMO files for all six
cycles: 59,842 values, 59,842 distinct. But the gap matters too — someone will try to
recover the cycle arithmetically from the ID, and that fails.
:::

# Thursday, previewed: L1 builds exactly this

## L1 in one screen: two files, one key

```r
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, nhanesA, tableone, naniar)

demo <- nhanes("DEMO_H", translated = TRUE)   # 2013-2014 demographics
bmx  <- nhanes("BMX_H",  translated = TRUE)   # 2013-2014 body measures

merged <- full_join(demo, bmx, by = "SEQN")
```

- `DEMO_H` and `BMX_H` are the **same** `DEMO` and `BMX` from the *"Where the measurements
  and labs come from"* table, cycle **H**
- `translated = TRUE` turns stored codes into labels — convenient, and it changes what a
  value *looks* like, so recode rules written against raw codes will silently miss
- **`full_join` keeps people measured in one file but not the other.** That is a row-set
  decision made by a single word: `inner_join` would be a different study

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Put the code on screen and read it aloud. The third bullet is the course's own
rule arriving in a one-line form: the join verb defines the analysis set, and swapping it
changes N without changing a single measurement. Ask them which verb they would want and
why — there is no universally right answer, which is the point.
:::

## Then do it for every cycle

```r
cycles <- c("H", "I", "J")                     # 2013-14, 2015-16, 2017-18

all_cycles <- lapply(cycles, function(cy) {
  d <- nhanes(paste0("DEMO_", cy), translated = TRUE)
  b <- nhanes(paste0("BMX_",  cy), translated = TRUE)
  full_join(d, b, by = "SEQN") %>% mutate(cycle = cy)
})

stacked <- bind_rows(all_cycles)
```

- `paste0("DEMO_", cy)` is why the **suffix table** was worth memorising
- `bind_rows()` stacks cycles; the joins happen **within** a cycle first
- Our reproduction does the same over **all six** cycles, `E` through `J`

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The loop is the step that turns one cycle into a study. Flag the thing that bites
here and comes back in Q5: a variable that exists in later cycles may not exist in earlier
ones, so a column can appear mid-stack and `bind_rows()` will happily fill the rest with
NA. That is not missingness in the usual sense; it is a changing instrument.
:::

## Raw names in, analysis names out

```r
analysis <- stacked %>%
  rename(Sex = RIAGENDR, Age = RIDAGEYR,
         RaceEthnicity = RIDRETH3, BMI = BMXBMI) %>%
  filter(Age >= 20) %>%
  mutate(BMICat = cut(BMI, c(0, 18.5, 25, 30, Inf), right = FALSE,
                      labels = c("Underweight", "Normal weight", "Overweight", "Obese")))
```

- Every rename is a **decision you have to be able to defend**, not cosmetics
- **`right = FALSE` is not optional.** Without it `cut()` closes the intervals the other
  way and BMI exactly 30.0 lands in *Overweight* — one argument, and the categories are
  the mirror image of the ones you meant
- `BMICat` here uses the standard WHO cut-points. **The paper does not**: obesity at
  **BMI ≥ 30**, and **≥ 25** for Asian participants
- The lab keeps **age ≥ 20**; the paper says **age > 18**; our reproduction uses **≥ 18**

> Same variable, three eligibility rules, three different studies.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) This is the highest-value slide in the preview block. The same `BMXBMI` becomes a
different analysis variable depending on the question, and the three age rules are a live
demonstration that "adults" is not a definition. Point hard at `right = FALSE`: a boundary
convention buried in a default argument silently reassigns everyone sitting exactly on a
cut-point. Tell them to record which rule they used, every time.
:::

## Look at what is missing before you model it

```r
colSums(is.na(analysis))
naniar::gg_miss_var(analysis, show_pct = TRUE)

tab1_vars <- c("Age", "RaceEthnicity", "BMI", "BMICat")
CreateTableOne(vars = tab1_vars, data = analysis, strata = "Sex",
               addOverall = TRUE, test = FALSE)
```

- Missingness is **inspected first**, then decided about — never discovered inside a model
- `CreateTableOne` is the Table 1 you will rebuild for the paper's cohort in **M1**
- `test = FALSE` on purpose: a p-value comparing baseline groups answers no question anyone
  asked

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Close the preview block by naming what Thursday produces: one merged table, a
missingness picture, and a descriptive table. Everything in the rest of the term runs on
that object. Week 7 is where the missingness picture turns into a method.
:::

# Q2, continued — the population this paper defines

## Population: who is being studied?

### Adults with MASLD in NHANES, 2007–2018

**MASLD** = metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: excess liver fat
together with metabolic dysfunction.

> But nobody looked at a liver. **Steatosis was estimated by a formula.**

The study population is **not the general population**. Everyone in the main analysis
already meets the study's own definition of MASLD.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) The second point is the one students skate over: the population is defined by a
computation, so it can be recomputed, and therefore it can disagree. That is the hinge
into the next slide.
:::

## How MASLD was actually ascertained

Hepatic steatosis was **estimated** with the **Fatty Liver Index** (Bedogni 2006),
thresholded at **FLI ≥ 60**:

| FLI input | NHANES variable | Component |
|---|---|---|
| Triglycerides | `LBXTR` | `TRIGLY` |
| BMI | `BMXBMI` | `BMX` |
| GGT | `LBXSGTSI` | `BIOPRO` |
| Waist circumference | `BMXWAIST` | `BMX` |

The four enter a published logistic formula — **not a product of the four.** What matters
here is that the index is *computed*, from four variables in three component files.

Plus **at least one of five cardiometabolic criteria**: adiposity; raised glucose/HbA1c or
diabetes; raised blood pressure or treatment; raised triglycerides or treatment; low HDL.

So "MASLD" here is a **derived variable, not a diagnosis** — no imaging, no biopsy.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Do not let this land as criticism. Every population study of MASLD in NHANES this
decade faces the same constraint. What matters is that eligibility is *computed*, from
four named variables in three different component files — and Q3 will show two of those
four turning up again in the exposure.
:::

## The funnel, with a type on every row

| Step | N | Kind of step |
|---|---|---|
| NHANES 2007–2018 records | 59,842 | — |
| Age ≥ 18 | 36,580 | eligibility — drops 23,262 |
| In fasting subsample | 14,962 | **design** — drops 21,618 |
| FLI computable | 14,170 | missingness |
| Steatosis (FLI ≥ 60) | 6,052 | target population — drops 8,118 |
| MASLD (≥1 criterion) | 6,050 | target population |
| Mortality-linked | **6,048** | outcome ascertainment |

**After eligibility**, the two largest drops are **design** and **disease definition** —
and neither is missing data.

*Analysis set: locked mortality-linked cohort, N = 6,048.*

::: {.notes}
(4 min) A funnel shows N falling; the type column shows why, and the types are not
interchangeable. Keep the scoping exact: the age criterion removes more people than
anything else (23,262), but that is the study's own eligibility rule. *After* eligibility,
the two biggest drops are the fasting subsample and the disease definition — which is why
the printed drops are on the table rather than asserted. Week 7, the M1 deck and the
reproduction report all state it in this scoped form. Name the row-set label explicitly and
say why it is there: the full reconstructed file is 6,371, and the two are not the same
cohort.
:::

## What the funnel reveals

**Reproducibility note.** The published paper reports **~6,300** participants with MASLD;
this pipeline yields **6,048** mortality-linked participants.
*Analysis set: locked mortality-linked cohort, N = 6,048.*

The two numbers should not be presented as if they described the same cohort.

The paper also states eligibility as **age > 18**, while this reproduction uses
**age ≥ 18**. Small implementation differences like this are **recorded, not silently
harmonised**.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Tie back to the lab preview: they have just seen three different age rules on one
slide. Here is what that costs. The discipline being taught is recording the difference,
not resolving it — a reproduction that quietly adopts the other rule has destroyed its own
evidence.
:::

# Q3 — Exposure and comparison

## The exposure is constructed, not measured

The exposure is not one measurement. It is built in two steps:

`BMXWAIST` ÷ `BMXHT` → **waist-to-height ratio** · `BMXBMI` → **obesity category**

→ BMI category **×** WHtR category → **four phenotype groups**

- All three inputs come from **one component, `BMX`**, in the MEC exam — so a person
  missing the exam is missing the exposure entirely
- Contrast that with **eligibility**, which needs `BMX` **and** the laboratory
  (`LBXTR`, `LBXSGTSI`) — eligibility spans two settings, the exposure does not

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Emphasise "constructed": two continuous measurements, two thresholds, one 2×2.
Every one of those four choices is a place a replicator can diverge from the authors. The
second bullet is a correction to an earlier version of this deck, which said the exposure
spanned two settings — it does not; eligibility does.
:::

## Exposure component 1: BMI

$$ \text{BMI} = \text{weight (kg)} / \text{height}^2 \text{ (m}^2\text{)} $$

- Weight and height were **measured** in the exam, not self-reported (`BMXBMI`)
- BMI marks **overall body size** — not body fat, and not where fat is stored
- Obesity defined as **BMI ≥ 30**; for Asian participants **BMI ≥ 25** (`RIDRETH3 == 6`)

> **Paper reporting note.** The Methods define obesity as BMI ≥ 30 (≥ 25 for Asian
> participants), but published Tables 1–2 label the groups as BMI ≥ 25 versus < 25. Those
> labels conflict with the Methods *and* with the reported group BMI distributions, so they
> appear to be a reporting error.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) The reporting note is a live demonstration of Q3 doing work: the exposure
definition appears twice in one paper and the two versions disagree. Ask them which one
they would implement, and how they would say so in writing. Flag `RIDRETH3` — it returns
in the traps slide, because it does not exist in the first two cycles.
:::

## Exposure component 2: waist-to-height ratio

$$ \text{WHtR} = \text{waist (cm)} / \text{height (cm)} = \texttt{BMXWAIST} / \texttt{BMXHT} $$

A person 170 cm tall with a 102 cm waist has WHtR = 102/170 = **0.60**.

- High central adiposity is defined as **WHtR ≥ 0.60**
- WHtR is a simple marker of **abdominal adiposity** — not CT or MRI visceral fat

::: {.notes}
(2 min) The worked arithmetic is there so the threshold stops being abstract. Note that
both inputs are on the same slide as BMI's inputs — one component file, three variables,
two derived quantities.
:::

## The exposure is the combination

|  | Lower central adiposity — WHtR < 0.60 | High central adiposity — WHtR ≥ 0.60 |
|---|---|---|
| **Obesity by BMI** | **Group I** — *reference* | **Group II** |
| **No obesity by BMI** | **Group III** | **Group IV** |

> **Group IV** — not obese by BMI, but a large waist for their height. The study asks
> whether BMI alone misses this higher-risk phenotype.

- There is no treated arm and control arm: the **four-category phenotype is the index
  factor**, and mortality is compared **across** the categories
- Every hazard ratio is measured **against Group I**. A ratio without its referent means
  nothing — and here the referent is an **obese** group

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Make them say the comparison out loud: Group IV versus Group I is "not obese with
high central adiposity, versus obese with lower central adiposity". Students routinely
read "HR 2.9" without asking "against what?", and this referent is counterintuitive enough
that the habit gets built here.
:::

## Eligibility and exposure share their inputs

|  | Inputs |
|---|---|
| **Eligibility** (FLI ≥ 60) | triglycerides, GGT, **BMI**, **waist** |
| **Exposure** (phenotype group) | **BMI**, **waist** ÷ height |

> Being selected into the study and being placed in a phenotype group are **not independent
> events**. That is **structural dependence**.

For a causal question, conditioning on this selected population could open selection or
collider paths under some structures; for a prognostic question, it primarily defines a
selected target population. It is not automatically circularity, and not automatically bias.

*Never trust a label you have not recomputed.*

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Name it as structural dependence, not as a diagnosed bias — the paragraph is
deliberately conditional. What it does to an estimate depends on the research goal and the
causal structure, which is Q1 arriving with consequences. We name it today; M1 dissects it.
:::

# Q4 — Outcome, time zero, follow-up

## Outcome and the clock

- **All-cause mortality** (`MORTSTAT`) via the NCHS linked mortality file — *not* an NHANES
  file, a separate linked fixed-width one
- **Time zero is the MEC examination**; `PERMTH_EXM` is person-months from that exam
- Follow-up through **31 December 2019**, stated in the NCHS 2019 Linked Mortality File
  linkage methodology document — not inferred from the filename
- Participants entered between 2007 and 2018, so **follow-up lengths and censoring differ**
  — time-to-event methods are appropriate. A **risk difference at a fixed horizon can still
  be estimated**, using methods that account for censoring

::: {.notes}
(6 min) Two things to point at explicitly. First, the sourcing: we know the end date
because NCHS documents it, not because the filename says 2019 — that is the standard we
ask of them. Second, the last bullet is a correction: differing follow-up does not forbid
an absolute contrast, it forbids a naive one.
:::

## Time zero is a question the checklist never asks

- "Exposure, outcome, covariates" can all be specified while **time zero stays ambiguous**
- An ambiguous time zero silently changes **who is at risk, and for how long**
- Here exposure is measured **at** time zero — convenient, and rarer than you would think

*Ask of your M0 candidates: when does follow-up begin, and does everyone start together?*

::: {.notes}
(5 min) This is one of the two places the six questions beat the old four primitives
outright. The primitives never forced this question, and it is where cohort studies most
often go quietly wrong. If you have time, ask for a show of hands on whether their
candidate papers state it.
:::

# Q5 — Other variables, and their roles

## "In the model" is not the same as "confounding"

- The paper adjusts for age, sex, comorbidities, medications
- **"We adjusted for X" says where X sits in the syntax. It does not say what X does.**
- The same variable can be a confounder, a mediator, a competing prognostic factor, or a
  collider — and which it is depends on the **research goal from Q1**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Q1 pays off again. Under a prognostic-factor question the adjustment set need not
be confounders at all; they may be other prognostic factors, included precisely so the
index factor has to earn its place beyond them.
:::

## What a crude-to-adjusted change establishes

- Group IV all-cause HR ≈ **15.1 crude → ≈ 2.9 adjusted**
- Conditioning on the adjustment set moves the estimate **enormously**
- What that movement *means* — confounding controlled, mediation removed, a collider
  opened — depends on the goal and the causal role of those variables

*Analysis set: full reconstructed analytic file, N = 6,371.*

::: {.notes}
(5 min) **Week 4 does this work.** Today it is enough that the size of a move is not itself
an interpretation. **Vote and argue:** what would you need to know to call this
confounding? Collect answers, resist supplying one — Week 4 is where the DAG logic arrives.
:::

## Five NHANES traps — each has bitten this project

- **`ALQ130` is drinks per *drinking day*, not drinks per day.** A ">2 a day" rule applied
  to it directly over-excluded roughly **2,000** people here — average intake needs
  frequency × quantity. **Week 3 owns this one**
- **777 = refused, 999 = don't know — codes, not counts.** Left inside a threshold rule
  they reclassified **nine** refusals as heavy drinkers. Two traps on one variable, a
  factor of two hundred apart
- **`RIDRETH3` does not exist before 2011.** It is what identifies Asian participants for
  the lower BMI threshold — so the first two cycles cannot apply the paper's own rule
- **Fasting labs carry their own weight.** `LBXTR` and `LBXGLU` come from the fasting
  subsample, weighted by `WTSAF2YR`, not `WTMEC2YR`
- **Blood pressure is not a row mean** — next slide

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Each of these cost this project real time, and each is a variable-handling
decision, which is why they sit under Q5 rather than in a separate "tips" section. The
first two are deliberately separated: an earlier version of this slide fused them and
attached the 2,000 to the reserved codes, which is wrong by a factor of two hundred. The
`RIDRETH3` one is the sharpest teaching point — a definition that cannot be applied in a
third of your cycles is a finding about the study, not a nuisance. For the record, the
alcohol numbers: the exclusion moves 2,063 → 2,072 when the reserved codes are left in.
Week 3 runs the full demonstration.
:::

## The blood pressure trap, in full

The NHANES **Blood Pressure Procedures Manual (s3.1.7.3)** specifies the averaging:

- The **first reading is excluded** whenever more than one was obtained
- An **all-zero diastolic set averages to zero** — a diastolic 0 is a *measurement*, and
  NHANES codes a failure to obtain a reading separately, as missing
- A **zero sitting beside a positive reading is omitted** from the average

Applying it changed derived SBP/DBP for **5,523 of 6,371** participants and moved
hypertension from 3,444 to 3,448 — while the adjusted hazard ratios shifted only in the
third significant figure. *Analysis set: full reconstructed analytic file, N = 6,371.*

> **A coding error can be real, and worth fixing, even when the headline estimate survives it.**

::: {.notes}
(3 min) This is the best available demonstration that "the result did not change" is not a
defence of a wrong implementation. Note also what the paper does *not* say: it does not
specify its own averaging in enough detail to establish that it used this algorithm, which
is why our version is a documentation-informed choice rather than a claim of exact
computational reproduction.
:::

# Q6 — Design and analysis features

## NHANES is not a simple random sample

- A complex multistage probability design: **weights**, **strata** (`SDMVSTRA`), **PSUs**
  (`SDMVPSU`)
- We *use* them in **Week 6**; today, note they exist and that ignoring them is a choice
- Fasting-subsample analyses carry their own weight — **`WTSAF2YR`**, not `WTMEC2YR`
- Build the design on the **full frame**, then `subset()` — never on the subsample alone

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Do not teach the survey mechanics here; Week 6 owns them. The Q6 point is that a
design feature exists and a Methods section should say how it was handled. The last bullet
is the single most common survey-analysis error and it is worth planting now.
:::

## Designed subsampling is not missingness

- The fasting subsample is **statistically designed**, not self-selected, and carries a
  weight built to keep it nationally representative
- Check rather than assume: adults in and out of it differ by **0.2 years of age,
  0.02 kg/m² BMI, 0.07 cm waist**
- It is balanced on the very measurements this paper's exposure is built from

*Analysis set: all NHANES adults 2007–2018, N = 36,580.*

> **Designed subsampling ≠ ordinary missingness.**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) An earlier version of this lecture taught the fasting subsample as a preview of
selection bias. That was wrong, and the measured balance above is why. The distinction
worth teaching is design versus missingness — and the fact that it was checked, rather
than assumed in either direction, is the transferable habit.
:::

## Survey design: paper versus reproduction

- The published paper's **Statistical analysis section does not report** using NHANES
  survey weights, strata or PSUs
- Our pipeline **does** include design variables and the fasting-subsample weight
- Therefore a survey-weighted rebuild is a **design-informed reanalysis**, not a literal
  reproduction of every published analytic choice

> Without the design information, estimates and standard errors should not be described as
> design-based nationally representative estimates.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Close Q6 by naming it as the question answered by omission. This is also the
cleanest example in the course of a difference that is neither an error by us nor an error
by them — it is a documented divergence, and the honest move is to label it as one.
:::

# Closing

## PECOT, and the question rebuilt

| Element | This study |
|---|---|
| **P** — Population | Adults with MASLD by FLI ≥ 60 + ≥1 cardiometabolic criterion, in the fasting subsample |
| **E** — Exposure | Four-category BMI × WHtR phenotype |
| **C** — Comparison | Groups II, III, IV versus **Group I** |
| **O** — Outcome | All-cause mortality to 31 Dec 2019 |
| **T** — Time | Months from exam to death or censoring |

> Among adults with MASLD, are BMI/WHtR phenotypes associated with different subsequent
> risks of all-cause mortality?

::: {.notes}
(2 min) The wording makes population, exposure, comparison, outcome and time explicit —
and is honest about how the population was defined. That sentence is the deliverable shape
for M0.
:::

## M0 — ask the six of your own papers

- Shortlist two or three candidate NHANES papers; answer **all six**, each with a pointer
  to where in the paper you found it
- **Reconstructable is necessary, not sufficient** — a perfectly specified paper can still
  be a poor M0 choice
- M0 wants: enough observations and events, a design feature its analysis must respect, and
  a missing variable the analysis actually uses
- An unanswered question is not a disqualification — it is a candidate for the judgement
  you defend at **M1**

::: {.notes}
(2 min) If you are ahead of schedule, work one candidate live — it is the single most
useful thing you can do with spare minutes. The six answers plus pointers are the M0
deliverable's spine.
:::

## Bridge to L1 and M0

- **Thursday (L1):** the code you saw before the break — several cycles downloaded, topic
  files read, merged on `SEQN`, renamed, categorised, missingness inspected, Table 1 built
- **Before you go:** you should be able to name the component file each variable on these
  slides comes from
- **Toward M0 (Wk3):** bring six answers per candidate paper, not a summary

*Reading a Methods section is the first act of reproduction.*

::: {.notes}
(2 min) Send them to L1 knowing exactly which files they are merging and why. The middle
bullet is a genuine self-test — ask two or three at random on the way out.
:::
